detail.abstract_excerpt: Real-world portfolio management requires converting noisy market observations into coordinated, simultaneous allocations across multiple assets under shared capital constraints. Advances in forecasting models and alpha discovery help identify opportunities. However, traditional pipelines often decouple signal forecasting from portfolio construction, potentially misaligning learning with allocation and execution objectives. We present AllocFlow, an end-to-end flow-matching framework that directly generates joint portfolio allocations from raw multi-asset market histories. To capture dependencies among portfolio positions, AllocFlow employs a cross-asset flow Transformer conditioned on temporal market representations to generate continuous, signed position weights across all instruments jointly. To address the sample inefficiency and instability of learning continuous allocation policies from scratch, we establish a two-stage training scheme: strategy-supervised imitation shapes a structured distribution of candidate portfolios, followed by group-relative reinforcement learning (RL) that refines joint decisions using portfolio-level financial rewards and a frozen policy reference. On hourly cryptocurrency perpetual futures, RL refinement raises the annualized net return of the imitation policy from $27.79\%$ to $51.38\%$ and its Calmar ratio from $0.955$ to $4.043$, surpassing the teacher strategy on every metric, and AllocFlow reaches a Calmar ratio of $4.90$ on six further months of unseen 2026 data without retraining.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Continuous autoregressive TTS relies on an acoustic target that enables stable next-latent modeling while preserving fine-grained acoustic details. While existing approaches employ learned compressed representations (e.g., continuous VAE latents) to render prediction tractable, they rely on complex neural encoders that often cap generation fidelity. Conversely, training-free targets like mel-spectrograms eliminate encoder overhead, yet their potential for autoregressive generation remains largely underexplored. In this work, we propose VoxMel, a tokenizer-free framework for autoregressive TTS that makes stable mel modeling tractable through a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform. The transform first decomposes each mel spectrogram along frequency into local averages and a frequency residual, then splits the averaged component along time into Coarse-Mel and a temporal residual. A language-model backbone with a flow-matching head autoregressively generates Coarse-Mel. Non-autoregressive residual tiers then predict the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel, followed by the frequency residual conditioned on the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel. Neither residual is fed back into the autoregressive history. Trained on 100K hours of Emilia, the supervised 0.6B model obtains 1.51\% WER and 0.738 speaker similarity (SIM) on test-en, and 1.29\% CER and 0.755 SIM on test-zh. GRPO improves these results to 1.15\% WER / 0.753 SIM and 1.17\% CER / 0.776 SIM, respectively. We also distill the guided flow head into two- and four-step students, requiring 2 or 4 head evaluations per coarse frame. The four-step student retains competitive SIM and nearly matches the supervised model in WER/CER.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Imagine halving the resource costs of AI and what that could mean for the planet and the industry -- based on extreme estimates such savings could reduce the total US power usage by over 10% by 2030 1 . At Intel we've been creating a new analyzer tool to help reduce AI costs called AI Flame Graphs : a visualization that shows an AI accelerator or GPU hardware profile along with the full software stack, based on my CPU flame graphs . Our first version is available to customers in the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (previously called Ponte Vecchio). Here is an example: Simple example: SYCL matrix multiply microbenchmark (Click for interactive SVG .) The green frames are the actual instructions running on the AI or GPU accelerator, aqua shows the source code for these functions, and red (C), yellow (C++), and orange (kernel) show the CPU code paths that initiated these AI/GPU programs. The gray "-" frames just help highlight the boundary between CPU and AI/GPU code. The x-axis is proportional to cost, so you look for the widest things and find ways to reduce them. Layers This flame graph shows a simple program for SYCL (a high-level C++ language for accelerators) that tests three implementations of matrix multiply, running them with the same input workload. The flame graph is dominated by the slowest implementation, multiply_basic(), which doesn't use any optimizations and consumes at 72% of stall samples and is shown as the widest tower. On the right are two thin towers for multiply_local_access() at 21% which replaces the accessor with a local variable, and multiply_local_access_and_tiling() at 6% which also adds matrix tiling. The towers are getting smaller as optimizations are added. This flame graph profiler is a prototype based on Intel EU stall profiling for hardware profiling and eBPF for software instrumentation. It's designed to be easy and low-overhead , just like a CPU profiler. You should be able to generate a flame graph of an existing AI workload whenever you want, without having to restart anything or launch additional code via an interposer. Instruction-offset Profiling This is not the first project to build an AI profiler or even something called an AI Flame Graph, however, others I've seen focus on tracing CPU stacks and timing accelerator execution, but don't profile the instruction offsets running on the accelerator; or do profile them but via expensive binary instrumentation. I wanted to build AI flame graphs that work like CPU flame graphs: Easy to use, negligible cost, production safe, and shows everything. A daily tool for developers, with most of the visualization in the language of the developer : source code functions. This has been an internal AI project at Intel for the past year. Intel was already investing in this space, building the EU stall profiler capability for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series that provides an approximation of HW instruction sampling. I was lucky to have Dr. Matthew (Ben) Olson , an Intel AI engineer who has also worked on eBPF performance tooling ( processwatch ) as well as memory management research, join my team and do most of the development work. His background has helped us power through difficulties that seemed insurmountable. We've also recently been joined by Dr. Brandon Kammerdiener (coincidentally another graduate of the University of Tennessee, like Ben), who also has eBPF and memory internals experience, and has been helping us take on harder and harder workloads. And Gabriel Muñoz just joined today to help with releases. Now that our small team has shown that this is possible, we'll be joined by other teams at Intel to develop this further. We could have built a harder-to-use and higher-overhead version months ago using Intel GTPin but for widespread adoption it needs minimal overhead and ease of use so that developers don't hesitate to use this daily and to add it to deployment pipelines. What's a Flame Graph? A flame graph is a visualization I invented in 2011 for showing sampled code stack traces. It has become the standard for CPU profiling and analysis, helping developers quickly find performance improvements and eliminate regressions. A CPU flame graph shows the "big picture" of running software, with x-axis proportional to CPU cost. The example picture on the right summarizes how easy it can be to go from compute costs to responsible code paths. Prior to flame graphs, it could take hours to understand a complex profile by reading through hundreds of pages of output . Now it takes seconds: all you have to do is look for the widest rectangles. Flame graphs have had worldwide adoption. They have been the basis for five startups so far, have been adopted in over thirty performance analysis products, and have had over eighty implementations . My first implementation of flame graphs took a few hours on a Wednesday night after work. The real effort has been in the decade since, where I worked with different profilers, runtimes, libraries, kernels, compilers, and hypervisors to get flame graphs working properly in different environments, including fixing stack walking and symbolization. Earlier this year I posted about the final missing piece: Helping distros enable frame pointers so that profiling works across standard system libraries. Similar work is necessary for AI workloads: fixing stacks and symbols and getting profiling to work for different hardware, kernel drivers, user-mode drivers, frameworks, runtimes, languages, and models. A lot more work, too, as AI analysis has less maturity than CPU analysis. Searching Samples If you are new to flame graphs, it's worth mentioning the built-in search capability. In the earlier example, most of the stall samples are caused by sbid: software scoreboard dependency. As that may be a unique search term, you can run search (Ctrl-F, or click "Search") on "sbid" and it will highlight it in magenta: Search also shows the total number of stack samples that contained sbid in the bottom right: 78.4%. You can search for any term in the flame graph: accelerator instructions, source paths, function names, etc., to quickly calculate the percentage of stacks where it is present (excluding vertical overlap) helping you prioritise performance work. Note that the samples are EU stall-based, which means theoretical performance wins can take the percentages down to zero. This is different to timer-based samples as are typically used in CPU profiling. Stalls mean you better focus on the pain, the parts of the code that aren't making forward progress, but you aren't seeing resource usage by unstalled instructions. I'd like to supuport timer-based samples in the future as well, so we can have both views. Who will use this? At a recent golang conference, I asked the audience of 200+ to raise their hands if they were using CPU flame graphs. Almost every hand went up. I know of companies where flame graphs are a daily tool that developers use to understand and tune their code, reducing compute costs. This will become a daily tool for AI developers. My employer will use this as well for evaluation analysis, to find areas to tune to beat competitors, as well as to better understand workload performance to aid design. Why is AI profiling hard? Consider CPU instruction profiling: This is easy when the program and symbol table are both in the file system and in a standardized file format (such as ELF) as is the case with native compiled code (C). CPU profiling gets hard for JIT-complied code, like Java, as instructions and symbols are dynamically generated and placed in main memory (the process heap) without following a universal standard. For such JITted code we use runtime-specific methods and agents to retrieve snapshots of the heap information, which is different for each runtime. AI workloads also have different runtimes (and frameworks, languages, user-mode drivers, compilers, etc.) any of which can require special tinkering to get their CPU stacks and symbols to work. These CPU stacks are shown as the red, orange, and yellow frames in the AI Flame Graph. Some AI workloads are easy to get these frames working, some (like PyTorch) are a lot more work. But the real challenge is instruction profiling of actual GPU and AI accelerator programs -- shown as the aqua and green frames -- and correctly associating them with the CPU stacks beneath them. Not only may these GPU and AI programs not exist in the file system, but they may not even exist in main memory! Even for running programs. Once execution begins, they may be deallocated from main memory and only exist in special accelerator memory, beyond the direct reach of OS profilers and debuggers. Or within reach, but only through a prohibitively high-overhead HW-specific debugger interface. There's also no /proc representation for these programs either (I've been proposing building an equivalent) so there's no direct way to even tell what is running and what isn't, and all the other /proc details. Forget instruction profiling, even ps(1) and all the other process tools do not work. It's been a mind-bending experience, revealing what gets taken for granted because it has existed in CPU land for decades: A process table. Process tools. Standard file formats. Programs that exist in the file system. Programs running from main memory. Debuggers. Profiliers. Core dumping. Disassembling. Single stepping. Static and dynamic instrumentation. Etc. For GPUs and AI, this is all far less mature. It can make the work exciting at times, when you think something is impossible and then find or devise a way. Fortunately we have a head start as some things do exist. Depending on the runtime and kernel driver, there are debug interfaces where you can list running accelerator programs and other statistics, as used by tools like intel_gpu_top(1). You can kill -9 a GPU workload using intel_gpu_abrt(1). Some interfaces can even generate basic ELF files for the running accelerator programs that you can try to load in a debugger like gdb(1). And there is support for GPU/AI program disassembly, if you can get your hands on the binary. It feels to me like GPU/AI debugging, OS style, is about two years old. Better than zero, but still early on, and lots more ahead of us. A decade, at least. What do AI developers think of this? We've shown AI Flame Graphs to other AI developers at Intel and a common reaction is to be a bit puzzled, wondering what to do with it. AI developers think about their bit of code, but with AI Flame Graphs they can now see the entire stack for the first time, including the HW, and many layers they don't usually think about or don't know about. It basically looks like a pile of gibberish with their code only a small part of the flame graph. CPU Flame Graph Implementations This reaction is similar to people's first experiences with CPU flame graphs, which show parts of the system that developers and engineers typically don't work on, such as runtime internals, system libraries, and kernel internals. Flame graphs are great at highlighting the dozen or so functions that matter the most, so it becomes a problem of learning what those functions do across a few different code bases, which are typically open source. Understanding a dozen such functions can take a few hours or even a few days -- but if this leads to a 10% or 2x cost win, it is time well spent. And the next time the user looks at a flame graph, they start saying "I've seen that function before" and so on. You can get to the point where understanding the bulk of a CPU flame graph takes less than a minute: look for the widest tower, click to zoom, read the frames, done. I'm encouraged by the success of CPU flame graphs, with over 80 implementations and countless real world case studies. Sometimes I'm browsing a performance issue I care about on github and hit page down and there's a CPU flame graph. They are everywhere. I expect AI developers will also be able to understand AI Flame Graphs in less than a minute, but to start with people will be spending a day or more browsing code bases they didn't know were involved. Publishing case studies of found wins will also help people learn how to interpret them, and also help explain the value. What about PyTorch? Another common reaction we've had is that AI developers are using PyTorch, and initially we didn't support it as it meant walking Python stacks, which isn't trivial. But prior work has been done there (to support CPU profiling) and after a lot of tinkering we now have the first PyTorch AI Flame Graph: PyTorch frames in pink (Click for interactive SVG .) The PyTorch functions are at the bottom and are colored pink. This example runs oneDNN kernels that are JIT-generated, and don't have a source path so that layer just reads "jit". Getting all other the layers included was a real pain to get going, but an important milestone. We think if we can do PyTorch we can do anything. In this flame graph, we show PyTorch running the Llama 2 7B model using the Intel Extensions for PyTorch (IPEX). This flame graph shows the origin of the GPU kernel execution all the way back to the Python source code shown in pink. Most samples are from a stack leading up to a gemm_kernel (matrix multiply) shown in aqua, which like the previous example has many stalls due to software scoreboarding. There are two instructions (0xa30 and 0xa90) that combined are 27% of the entire profile. I expect someone will ask: Can't we just click on instructions and have it bring up a dissassembly view with full source? Yes, that should be possible, but I can't answer how we're going to provide this yet. Another expected question I can't yet answer: Since there are now multiple products providing AI auto-tuning of CPU workloads using CPU flame graphs (including Intel Granulate ) can't we have AI auto-tuning of AI workloads using AI Flame Graphs? First Release: Sometimes hard and with moderate overhead Getting AI Flame Graphs to work with some workloads is easy, but others are currently hard and cost moderate overhead. It's similar to CPU profiling, where some workloads and languages are easy to profile, whereas others need various things fixed. Some AI workloads use many software dependencies that need various tweaks and recompilation (e.g., enabling frame pointers so that stack walking works) making setup time consuming. PyTorch is especially difficult and can take over a week of OS work to be ready for AI Flame Graphs. We will work on getting these tweaks changed upstream in their respective repositories, something involving teams inside and outside of Intel, and is a process I'd expect to take at least a year. During that time AI workloads will gradually become easier to flame graph, and with lower-overhead as well. I'm reminded of eBPF in the early days: You had to patch and recompile the kernel and LLVM and Clang, which could take multiple days if you hit errors. Since then all the eBPF dependency patches have been merged, and default settings changed, so that eBPF "just works." We'll get there with AI Flame Graphs too, but right now it's still those early days. The changes necessary for AI Flame Graphs are really about improving debugging in general, and are a requirement for Fast by Friday : A vision where we can root-cause analyze anything in five days or less. Availability AI Flame Graphs will first become available on the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview feature for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series. If you are currently deployed there you can ask through the Intel service channel for early access. As for if or when it will support other hardware types, be in other Intel products, be officially launched, be open source, etc., these involve various other teams at Intel and they need to make their own announcements before I can discuss them here. Conclusions Finding performance improvements for AI data centers of just fractions of a percent can add up to planetary savings in electricity, water, and money. If AI flame graphs have the success that CPU flame graphs have had, I'd expect finding improvements of over 10% will be common, and 50% and higher will eventually be found*. But it won't be easy in these early days as there are still many software components to tweak and recompile, and software layers to learn about that are revealed in the AI flame graph. In the years ahead I imagine others will build their own AI flame graphs that look the same as this one, and there may even be startups selling them, but if they use more difficult-to-use and higher-overhead technologies I fear they could turn companies off the idea of AI flame graphs altogether and prevent them from finding sorely needed wins. This is too important to do badly. AI flame graphs should be easy to use, cost negligible overhead, be production safe, and show everything. Intel has proven it's possible. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out. We study how such policies affect creator displacement in a model of a platform where creators choose whether to contribute training data and consumers choose between purchasing from creators and prompting generative AI trained on their content. This constraint also prevents further AI displacement as AI improves, with the platform raising AI prices while keeping creators' prices and demand unchanged to prevent exit. Compensation increases creators' payoffs and total surplus but reduces consumer surplus. Our findings highlight how compensation policies for training data can shape creators' economic roles in a future with more capable generative AI.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Nash equilibrium and rationalizability sit at opposite informational extremes: the former presumes that each player knows all opponents' strategies, the latter that players reason from common knowledge of rationality alone. When visibility is partial and asymmetric, we study the solution concepts induced by a directed \emph{observation network} $G$ in which an edge $i\to j$ means that $i$ observes $j$'s strategy. A set of profiles is \emph{self-sustaining} if every profile in it can be justified, for every player, by conjectures from the same set that agree with everything the player observes. We consider \emph{point} conjectures (single profiles) and \emph{belief} conjectures (distributions over profiles). Both range from Nash equilibrium on the complete network to point- and correlated rationalizability on the empty network, and shrink monotonically as links are added. Network topology governs both behavior and complexity. A predicted profile can be found in polynomial time on the empty network, whereas a single link makes search $\mathsf{PPAD}$-hard: under one-sided two-player monitoring, the observed player's strategies are exactly her Nash equilibrium strategies. On hierarchical networks (transitive tournaments), membership reduces recursively to smaller games and admits polynomial-size certificates, placing verification in $\exists\mathbb{R}$, and in $\mathsf{P}$ for two players. On the directed three-cycle, however, iterated elimination may never terminate under either variant, and under point conjectures interior predictions may admit only infinite witness sets, a pathology that belief conjectures avoid in the same game. Finally, when only realized pure actions are observed, the solution set is guaranteed to be non-empty exactly when the network has no edges, and is computable in time $O(n|A|^2)$.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Antiferromagnets on the hyperkagome lattice provide a three-dimensional route to strong magnetic frustration, but experimentally accessible realizations with well-established microscopic Hamiltonians remain scarce. Garnets are a broad family of materials in which magnetic ions can form two interpenetrating hyperkagome lattices, giving rise to spin glass, spin-liquid and hidden-order physics. Here we identify the iron aluminosilicate garnet almandine, Fe$_3$Al$_2$Si$_3$O$_{12}$, as a spin-$2$ hyperkagome antiferromagnet. Using density functional theory energy mapping, we determine a Heisenberg Hamiltonian for the high-spin Fe$^{2+}$ moments and find dominant nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic exchange, as well as significant longer-range interactions. Classical Monte Carlo simulations of this Hamiltonian, combined with quantum-to-classical rescaling of the spin length, show a transition to antiferromagnetic order at $T_{\rm N}\approx9.8$K, in excellent agreement with specific heat experiments. The resulting non-collinear magnetic state is naturally described by magnetic toroidal octupolar order, which we connect to known results for the highly frustrated hyperkagome antiferromagnet gadolinium gallium garnet, Gd$_3$Ga$_5$O$_{12}$. We also calculate magnetic neutron diffraction amplitudes as well as static and dynamic structure factors using semiclassical dynamics, providing quantitative predictions for future neutron scattering experiments. detail.abstract_excerpt: Geometry enters quantum theory in two places. The space of quantum states carries a symplectic form, which generates unitary evolution, and a metric, which governs uncertainties and transition probabilities. The classical phase space acquires a metric of its own when a vacuum is chosen: quantizing a linear system amounts to choosing a compatible complex structure, equivalently a compatible metric $g$. We take this second metric as the primary object and show that it plays, on phase space, the role that the quantum metric plays on the space of states: fluctuations of linear observables are $g$-norms of Hamiltonian vector fields, and along coherent states $g/2\hbar$ \emph{is} the quantum metric. Squeezed states then have a simple description. A squeezed vacuum is the vacuum of another metric, and squeezing is a property of a pair of metrics, a relative vacuum, whose invariants are the eigenvalues $e^{\pm2r_i}$ of $L=g_0^{-1}g$. We work out the harmonic oscillator in detail, including why a rotated squeezed state no longer minimizes the product of the displayed uncertainties. Quadratic evolution deforms the metric, and only the part of the generator that is self-adjoint with respect to the reference changes the $r_i$, at a rate we give exactly. For fields, a vacuum is unitarily implementable relative to a reference exactly when it lies at finite distance from it in the space of vacua. For a massless field in de Sitter space we revisit the two canonical charts compared by Grain and Vennin: relative to the reference of the standard squeezing formalism the Bunch--Davies state has $\sinh r_k=1/(2|kη|)$, and relative to the vacuum that a radiation era beginning at time $η$ would select it has $\sinh r_k=1/(2k^2η^2)$. The second comparison squeezes twice as fast and is unitarily implementable; the first is not.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Single-pulse all-optical helicity-independent switching (AO-HIS) is most commonly observed in Gd-based ferrimagnets near magnetization compensation. Recent experiments, however, demonstrated switching in Pt/Co/Pt-based heterostructures containing only a small amount of Gd at a Co/Pt interface. We compare a three-monolayer Co film with Gd confined to the surface layer and a three-dimensional uniformly alloyed GdCo model. Within the present uniform-heating model, robust transient toggle-like reversal is obtained far from compensation when the Gd coupling to the thermal bath is substantially weaker than that of Co; for λCo = 0.02 and λCo = 0.001, reversal occurs down to 1.5 at. % total Gd for selected pulse parameters. Increasing the Gd content accelerates reversal, consistent with the interpretation of Gd as an angular-momentum reservoir, whereas dilute interfacial Gd produces slower and more stochastic dynamics. These results show that compensation is not a fundamental requirement for ultrafast AO-HIS and identify the effective Gd spin-bath coupling as a key control parameter. Quantitative comparison with experiment will require explicit optical absorption, stack-dependent heat flow, dipolar fields, and a stable-final-state switching criterion.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Why does symmetric sum-pooling (DeepSets) predict ground-state potentials to sub-meV accuracy, yet fail for correlated wavefunctions and excited states? Sum-pooling is a mean-field (Hartree) model: its $O(1/N)$ off-diagonal Jacobian suffices for nearsighted ground-state energies, but erases nonlocal two-body correlations. Because physical Hamiltonians act pairwise, Löwdin's 2-RDM theorem and the Galitskii--Migdal relation guarantee that iterating a two-body propagator captures the full energetics of correlated matter. When fitting a fractal backflow determinant, DeepSets blurs the nodal surface onto a mean-field envelope, whereas self-attention recovers the fractal attractor. Seen through this lens, the unreasonable effectiveness of attention is not an accident; in a universe built from pairwise interactions, two-body attention is all you need.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The key agreements that protect a Wi-Fi connection rely on Diffie-Hellman, which a sufficiently capable quantum computer would break; an adversary can therefore record an association today and decrypt its traffic years later. Key establishment is thus the part of IEEE 802.11 that has to be migrated first. This work targets the two protocols that perform that agreement inside the frames used to set up the link: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), which encrypts otherwise open networks, and Fast Initial Link Setup (FILS), designed for fast connection in dense and mobile deployments. We propose replacing their Diffie-Hellman exchange with a hybrid one that runs the classical elliptic-curve agreement alongside ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and derives the master key from both secrets, so the connection stays protected as long as either component remains unbroken. The exchange reuses the frames each protocol already sends and adds no extra round trip; an access point can advertise the hybrid mode alongside classical OWE, and a station configured to require it refuses to associate without a completed post-quantum exchange. Binding the advertised capabilities to the derived key is specified as a design extension and is not part of the prototype. We validate the design with a working implementation on hostapd and wpa_supplicant: both endpoints derive the same key in every measured connection, with the two smaller parameter sets each enlarged association frame fits in a single frame even under a conservative 1500-byte fragmentation threshold, and the added connection time and computation stay below half a millisecond. The measurements are obtained on OWE; the design carries over to FILS, whose frame budget is left for specific measurement. Of the three ML-KEM parameter sets, the intermediate one offers the best balance between security level and size.

detail.abstract_excerpt: This paper develops computational algorithms for testing discrete-choice random utility models (RUM). The set of RUM-consistent choice probabilities forms a polytope, and existing computational methods rely on its vertex representation. We exploit alternative half-space (Block--Marschak inequalities) and network-flow representations to develop two methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers and a flow-based column-generation algorithm. Compared with current vertex-based methods, our algorithms are better suited to GPU implementation. We establish convergence guarantees and provide optimality certificates for all three algorithms. The resulting algorithms achieve $100$--$600\times$ speedups over existing methods. The solver based on our methods is publicly available on Github at \href{https://github.com/mingxiz/d-rum-testing-gpu}{\texttt{d-rum-testing-gpu}}.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's $[[360, 12, \leq 24]]$ code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. QECLean is available at https://github.com/Stavan-Jain/QECLean

detail.abstract_excerpt: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed 1 , fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded. Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits 2 , are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table. Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below. Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures. Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats. As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future. Simulating malicious package repositories Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server. Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another. The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package. uuid : dependency : "direct main" description : name : uuid sha256 : "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd" url : "https://pub.dev" source : hosted version : "4.6.0" If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated. This is documented behavior , and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation 6 . Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected. Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++. "requires" : [ "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337" ] , This includes the package name ( zlib ), the version number ( 1.3.1 ), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20 , and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository. "source" : { "git" : "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git" , "tag" : "4.0.2" } , So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag. Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt. "dist" : { "type" : "zip" , "url" : "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "reference" : "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "shasum" : "" } , However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer. Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. detail.abstract_excerpt: Zero-knowledge proofs have become a fundamental tool for verifiable computation and privacy-preserving applications, driving growing interest in proof systems that are both succinct and efficient. In polynomial-based arguments, however, achieving zero knowledge introduces additional costs. Random masks must hide the evaluations and intermediate messages revealed during verification while preserving the underlying computation. Existing approaches range from protecting individual messages with cryptographic commitments to constructing small masking polynomials tailored to particular protocols. These techniques raise a more general question: how much randomness is needed when the verifier observes only a structured collection of evaluations and linear combinations? We present GoZK, a query-aware approach to zero knowledge that constructs masking spaces from the verifier’s conditional joint observations. We characterize these observations through affine images and develop low-degree masks for selected Cartesian strata, witness polynomials, and product-tree relations. In particular, two product trees that reveal eight boundary evaluations and a single root difference admit a nine-dimensional masking space, matching the dimension of their specified uniform observation interface. We integrate these constructions with a causal masking polynomial, a global sumcheck, and a pairing-based polynomial commitment scheme. The resulting protocol admits exact online simulation under the stated setup and private-coin conditions, with classical knowledge soundness established in a registered algebraic-group and random-oracle model. In a Rust implementation over BLS12-381, query-aware masking reduces the number of source-mask coefficients from 390 to 19 relative to an implemented projected arbitrary-point construction, saves 4,128 proof bytes, and improves prover time by factors of 1.40–1.67 on matched eight-column instances. Global sumcheck further reduces communication by 6,752–10,400 bytes, with a modest prover-time tradeoff.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Traceable secret sharing complements traditional schemes by enabling the identification of parties who sell their shares. More precisely, a group of corrupted parties generates a reconstruction box $R$ that, given enough valid shares as input, reconstructs the secret. The goal is to trace $R$ back to at least one of the corrupted parties using only black-box access to it. Recently, two independent works extended traceable secret sharing to general access structures. Goyal, Jain, and Partap [EC'26] introduced a model in which $R$ is augmented with a label $I \subseteq [n]$ and is only required to distinguish between two secrets when queried with the shares of parties in $I$. Based on how this label relates to the corrupted set $J$ that built the box, they defined two notions of traceability. If $I \cap J = \emptyset$, the model is called $\emptyset$-strong traceability, for which they presented a construction based on indistinguishability obfuscation (iO). Otherwise, their model is called strong traceability, for which they proved an impossibility result. Farràs and Guiot [EC'26] proposed a different model, which we call hidden traceability, where $R$ has no label and the access structure is hidden from the parties. In this work, we improve traceable secret sharing for general access structures in three directions. First, we present a fully information-theoretic scheme for the $\emptyset$-strong traceability model, eliminating the need for strong cryptographic assumptions. This resolves an open question posed by Goyal, Jain, and Partap, who asked what are the minimal assumptions needed in the $\emptyset$-strong traceability model. Second, motivated by the impossibility of strong traceability, we introduce a relaxed notion called hidden mildly strong traceability. This model is relevant in practice and bridges the strong and hidden models. For this setting, we present an information-theoretic scheme for general access structures. Finally, we consider the more general model of stateful traceability, where reconstruction boxes may keep state across queries, and we prove an impossibility result for this setting.

detail.abstract_excerpt: We improve differential-linear distinguishers and derive key-recovery attacks on reduced-round versions of the PRFs Orthros, Gleeok, ZIP-AES, ZIP-GIFT-64, and ZIP-GIFT-128. We also obtain distinguishers for 6-round Gleeok-256, $(3,3)$-round ZIP-AES, $(7,7)$-round ZIP-GIFT-64, and $(10,10)$-round ZIP-GIFT-128. For key recovery, we give a $(3,3)$-round differential-linear attack on ZIP-AES requiring approximately $2^{122.42}$ chosen plaintexts and $2^{122.88}$ ZIP-AES evaluations. The Orthros key-recovery result reaches one round beyond the previous DL key-recovery coverage. These results use automated differential and linear trail search together with existing round-based correlation estimation. Although using oblivious PRFs (OPRFs) can solve the over-revealing issue, doing so introduces additional trade-offs that may hinder practical deployment. We present a practical, hintless keyword PIR framework that natively eliminates over-revelation without relying on OPRFs, achieving symmetric PIR security. Building on KsPIR (CCS 2024) and the linearly homomorphic technique of Peikert and Pepin (TCC 2025), our server homomorphically evaluates key-value store decoding over encrypted queries, retrieving exactly the target record. To accelerate evaluation, we introduce a generalized baby-step giant-step (BSGS) algorithm for coefficient-encoded Galois sums, an offline/online decomposition, and a Horner-style evaluation chain that reduces uploaded evaluation keys to three. For databases up to $2^{22}$ entries, our construction achieves a mean online speedup of $2.65\times$ over their generic framework under the same index-PIR backend. Compared to their specialized design, our scheme attains comparable online time while requiring neither a client-side hint (saving 14.5--143.6 MB) nor an OPRF.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Falcon, a lattice-based signature scheme selected for NIST post-quantum standardization, is notable for its compact signature size alongside a complex signing procedure involving extensive floating-point arithmetic. Prior side-channel attacks on Falcon signing, while demonstrating vulnerabilities, have consistently required a large number of power traces for successful key recovery, which limits their real-world practicality. This paper presents a new single-trace attack on the Falcon signing procedure. We exploit side-channel leakage in the FP conversion and identify additional leakage in the FP multiplication at the first layer of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) during secret key expansion. By combining these leakages, we progressively partition the secret-key coefficients and establish a linear system to recover the entire key. Our attack is particularly devastating for the \texttt{sign\_dyn} design---the memory-efficient implementation widely adopted in cryptographic libraries---which executes key expansion during every signature operation. We validate our attack on an ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller, achieving a 100\% key recovery success rate with just one power trace for Falcon-512 across the baseline \texttt{-O0}, size-optimized \texttt{-Os}, and highest \texttt{-O3} compilation levels of the PQClean implementation. Crucially, we also evaluate the Falcon team's highly optimized embedded assembly (ASM) implementation. Despite its reduced leakage, our adapted multi-trace attack successfully recovers 53 out of 100 test keys with only 10 traces. This marks the first successful single-trace attack at the \texttt{-O3} level and the first practical attack against the embedded ASM Falcon. Furthermore, our in-depth assembly analysis of these vulnerabilities provides critical guidelines for designing more secure, hardened embedded assembly implementations.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Succinct arguments based on interactive oracle proofs (IOPs) have achieved remarkable efficiency improvements and are now widely adopted in applications. State-of-the-art IOPs involve protocols for testing proximity to constrained interleaved linear codes, and enjoy essentially optimal parameters. However, recent IOP constructions provide no privacy guarantees, which remain a must for many applications. We present an IOP of proximity for testing constrained interleaved linear codes that achieves (honest-verifier) zero-knowledge, while incurring a negligible overhead compared to the (non-zero-knowledge) state of the art. In line with recent constructions, our construction satisfies round-by-round knowledge soundness with a straightline extractor and negligible error. We propose a definition of (honest-verifier) zero-knowledge for interactive oracle reductions (IORs) that we prove is compatible with composition, and then obtain our result by constructing and modularly composing several lightweight zero-knowledge IORs. Our key technical contributions are a zero-knowledge sumcheck IOR and a zero-knowledge code-switching IOR that fit the strict efficiency requirements of our setting; these contributions and other technical complications entailed overcoming several challenges with new notions and protocols. Finally, along the way, we highlight the efficiency benefits of high-distance codes obtained from dispersers, which may be of independent interest.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Summary Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users.
